lesson.title: Thirteen Names, One Starting Line: The DNS Root
lesson.summary: Root name servers sit at the very top of the DNS hierarchy and answer every fresh lookup the same way: not with the final address, but with a referral to the right top level domain.
lesson.body:
Every resolution trace in this chapter set starts the same place: the root. Go back to the resolver's walk toward www.example.com. Its very first move, whenever nothing useful is cached, is to ask a root server, and the root server's job is deliberately narrow. It does not know the IP address for www.example.com, and it never will, because that information belongs to a zone far below it in the tree. What it does know is which organization runs the com TLD and where to find that organization's servers, so it answers with a referral rather than a final result.

There are thirteen root server names, labeled a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net, and they are operated independently by a mix of different organizations, including companies like Verisign and coordinating bodies like ICANN, rather than by one single entity. Thirteen names does not mean thirteen physical machines sitting in one room. Each of those names is anycast, meaning the same address is announced from many physical server locations scattered around the globe, so a query from nearly anywhere in the world reaches a nearby copy rather than traveling to one central location. This is both a performance choice, keeping the very first hop of every fresh lookup fast, and a resilience choice, since losing any single physical site does not take a root name off the internet.

The data root servers hand out barely changes and is tiny. The root zone is really just a list of delegations, one set of NS records for every TLD, com, org, edu, country codes, and so on, maintained under IANA and ICANN's oversight. It is the top level equivalent of the NS records you saw delegating example.com to its own authoritative servers, just one level higher and covering entire TLDs instead of a single domain.

Because that root zone is so small and so stable, its answers are extremely cacheable, and in practice most resolvers already have the referral to a given TLD sitting in cache and skip asking a root server at all. That efficiency, and exactly how it works, is the subject of the next chapter on DNS caching.
